concept.name: Release Train Cadence

relationships.description: Connects Release Train Cadence to canary deployments in the broader engineering catalog.

spark.summary: A release train is a fixed-schedule software delivery model where releases depart on a predictable calendar cadence—shipping whatever features are complete and verified, while incomplete work waits for the next train.
spark.keyTakeaway: Decouple deployment timing from feature completion: fix the release date, keep main deployable via feature flags, and never hold the train for one late pull request.

concept.whyItMatters: Ad-hoc, feature-driven releases trap engineering organizations in endless stabilization cycles: delaying a release for one unfinished feature piles up unshipped diffs, increases merge conflicts, and raises blast radius. A release train makes shipping routine, bounds batch size, and gives product, QA, and mobile app-review teams a reliable clock.
whenToUse: Multiple squads ship into a shared monorepo, mobile binary (iOS/Android), or coupled platform where coordinated integration testing is required.
External constraints—such as App Store/Play Store review windows (24–48 hours), enterprise customer change windows, or compliance sign-offs—prevent continuous per-commit deployment.
Releases frequently slip because teams negotiate scope at the last minute instead of shipping incremental, flag-gated work.
whenNotToUse: Independent microservices with automated contract tests and canary pipelines can already deploy safely multiple times per day via continuous deployment.
A small early-stage team (2–5 engineers) ships hotfixes and experiments continuously without cross-team coordination overhead.
The release requires a single-purpose security patch or P0 outage fix—emergency hotfixes should bypass the train via an expedited fast-track.
keyPoints: Schedule is fixed, scope is variable: the release branch cuts at a set day and time (e.g., every Tuesday 14:00 UTC) regardless of whether a specific feature finished.
Feature flags (LaunchDarkly, Unleash, or config flags) are mandatory so incomplete features can merge safely to trunk without exposing broken UX in the cut branch.
Each train follows predictable stages: branch cut, automated regression + soak testing, progressive canary rollout (1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%), and post-release monitoring.
Cherry-picks into a cut release branch must be strictly limited to verified P0/P1 regressions; adding features after branch cut destroys train predictability.
Train cadence should match verification cost: web/backend trains often run daily or weekly, while mobile app trains typically run weekly or biweekly.

examples.title: Biweekly Mobile App Release Train
examples.scenario: A 140-engineer fintech app ships iOS and Android binaries to 8M users, facing 24–48 hour App Store review delays and strict PCI regression suites.
examples.outcome: Cutting `release/2026.11` every other Monday at 10:00 UTC, running a 24-hour internal dogfood soak, and submitting Tuesday morning yields predictable Thursday 5%->100% phased rollouts and zero emergency scope-delay meetings.

examples.title: Weekly Platform & API Train
examples.scenario: A B2B SaaS platform with 12 backend teams suffered 4-hour Friday release war rooms and frequent rollbacks from bundled 3-week mega-releases.
examples.outcome: Moving to a weekly Tuesday train backed by Argo Rollouts (1% canary for 2 hours, automated error-budget gate) shrinks batch size by 3x and cuts rollback MTTR from 45 minutes to 8 minutes.

tradeOffs.pro: Shorter trains reduce batch size, limit blast radius, and lower the pressure to cram late changes onto a departing train.
tradeOffs.con: Frequent trains amplify fixed overhead if manual QA, changelog curation, or store approvals are not automated.

tradeOffs.factor: Strict branch-cut freeze vs. Permissive cherry-picking
tradeOffs.pro: Strict freezes preserve soak-test validity and keep release captains out of merge-conflict triage.
tradeOffs.con: Teams that miss the cut by an hour must wait a full cycle unless their change qualifies as a P0 fix.

tradeOffs.factor: Trunk-based + feature flags vs. Long-lived feature branches
tradeOffs.pro: Trunk-based integration eliminates painful merge-day hell and keeps every train buildable on schedule.
tradeOffs.con: Requires engineering discipline to clean up stale flags and test both flag-on and flag-off code paths.

failureModes.name: The 'One More PR' Anti-Pattern
failureModes.description: Product or engineering leaders repeatedly delay the branch cut or cherry-pick late features, turning a fixed train into a slipping ad-hoc release.
failureModes.mitigation: Enforce automated branch cuts via CI (GitHub Actions/GitLab CI) and require VP/EM sign-off for any post-cut cherry-pick.

failureModes.name: Cherry-Pick Avalanche
failureModes.description: Fixing bugs on main and cherry-picking dozens of commits onto the release branch invalidates earlier QA sign-off and introduces new regressions.
failureModes.mitigation: Restrict cherry-picks to P0/P1 blockers, require a green CI run on the release branch per pick, and reset soak timers on risky changes.

failureModes.name: Flag Debt Explosion
failureModes.description: Teams merge half-built features behind flags to catch the train but never remove old flags, creating combinatorial config bugs.
failureModes.mitigation: Set a 30-day TTL on release flags, track flag age in CI/dashboards, and block new flag creation when stale-flag count exceeds threshold.

failureModes.name: Broken Main at Cut Time
failureModes.description: Flaky tests or un-reverted broken commits on trunk block the automated cut, stalling all teams simultaneously.
failureModes.mitigation: Use merge queues (GitHub Merge Queue / Bors) that test PRs against main before merge and enforce an immediate revert-first policy.

commonMistakes: Tying marketing launch dates directly to code-cut dates instead of decoupling code shipping from flag activation.
Assigning a permanent manual 'release hero' instead of rotating a lightweight Release Captain role supported by automated CI scripts.
Allowing database schema migrations that break backward compatibility with the previous train during rolling or canary deployments.
Skipping automated rollback triggers on canary error-rate or latency SLOs during phased rollouts.
Running a release train without measuring lead time, change failure rate, and cherry-pick count to detect process drift.

sections.content:
## The idea

A **release train** replaces variable-date, feature-gated releases with a **fixed-calendar, scope-variable** cadence. Like a commuter train, it leaves the station on a published schedule—say every Tuesday at 14:00 UTC—with whatever commits have already landed and passed CI on `main`.

If a feature is incomplete at cut time, it stays behind a **feature flag** (off by default) or remains on an unmerged branch and simply rides the next train. By making departure predictable and batch sizes bounded, teams eliminate last-minute integration crunch, shrink blast radius, and align QA, documentation, and app-store reviews to a steady rhythm.

## Concrete walkthrough

Here is how a **biweekly Tuesday release train** operates in a 100-engineer web + mobile organization:

1. **Continuous trunk integration (Days 1–10)**: Engineers merge small PRs to `main` via a GitHub Merge Queue. Incomplete work is wrapped in a LaunchDarkly flag (`enable_instant_payouts=false`).
2. **Automated branch cut (Tuesday 14:00 UTC)**: A scheduled GitHub Actions workflow tags `v2026.11.2`, creates `release/2026.11.2`, builds signed artifacts, and posts the auto-generated changelog to `#release-train`.
3. **Soak & verification (Wednesday)**: The release branch deploys to staging and internal dogfooding. Only P0/P1 bug fixes are cherry-picked from `main` via `/cherry-pick` bot commands.
4. **Progressive canary rollout (Thursday)**: Argo Rollouts (backend) and Play/App Store phased release shift traffic `1% -> 10% -> 50% -> 100%` over 24 hours, halting automatically if 5xx rate exceeds `0.5%` or crash-free sessions drop below `99.8%`.
5. **Flag ramp & cleanup (Following week)**: Product teams independently enable feature flags for customers and file cleanup PRs to retire flags within 14 days of 100% rollout.

sections.eyebrow: 03 / Choosing cadence and release captain governance
sections.content:
## Choosing cadence and release captain governance

The ideal train interval equals roughly **2x to 3x your end-to-end verification and rollout time**. If mobile store review and soak take 3 days, a weekly or biweekly train works cleanly; if backend CI + canary takes 45 minutes, daily trains or full continuous deployment are viable.

To avoid bottlenecks, rotate a **Release Captain** weekly across squads using a written runbook. The captain's job is not to debug code—it is to triage cherry-pick requests against a clear rubric (crash, security, or data loss only) and trigger rollbacks when canary SLOs breach.

## Delivery model comparison

| Model | Trigger | Batch Size | Coordination Cost | Best Fit |
| :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- | :--- |
| **Continuous Deployment** | Every green commit to `main` | 1 PR | Very Low | Decoupled web services & APIs with strong canarying |
| **Daily / Weekly Release Train** | Fixed calendar clock | 10–100 PRs | Low–Medium | Coupled monorepos, B2B SaaS, multi-squad backends |
| **Biweekly Mobile Train** | Fixed calendar + store review | 50–250 PRs | Medium | iOS/Android binaries with 24–48h store review gates |
| **Feature-Driven Release** | 'When feature X is done' | Unbounded | Very High | Legacy monoliths lacking feature flags (avoid if possible) |

## Failure modes and operational guardrails

Release trains degrade silently when teams treat the branch cut as a soft suggestion:

- **Scope creep via cherry-picks**: Track `cherry_picks_per_train`. If it exceeds 3–5 commits regularly, teams are either merging untested code right before cut or abusing cherry-picks to sneak in features.
- **Schema-version skew**: During canary rollouts, train `N` and train `N-1` run simultaneously. Enforce expand-and-contract migrations so new columns/endpoints are additive until train `N` reaches 100%.
- **Missed-train panic**: When a team misses Tuesday's cut, reassure them the next train is only days away—never delay the entire org's train for one feature.

## Automating the train

Healthy release trains automate every mechanical step: **merge queues** keep `main` green, **scheduled CI jobs** cut branches and bump semantic versions, **conventional commits** generate release notes, and **progressive delivery controllers** (Argo Rollouts, Flagger, or Play Console staged rollouts) halt or roll back automatically on Prometheus/Datadog SLO breaches. Manual effort should be reserved strictly for go/no-go exception calls.

## Practical checklist

- **Publish a fixed cut schedule**: Put the exact day, UTC time, and timezone-converted calendar invites in a shared team calendar.
- **Automate branch cutting & changelogs**: Never rely on a developer running local git scripts on their laptop.
- **Mandate feature flags for multi-PR work**: Require unfinished features to stay dark behind flags so `main` is always releasable.
- **Enforce expand-contract DB migrations**: Guarantee backward compatibility with the prior release during canary overlap.
- **Track train health metrics**: Monitor cherry-pick count, cut delays, rollback rate, and stale flag age every sprint.

interviewProblems.title: Release Train Cadence
interviewProblems.scenarioPrompt: Design a production system that depends on Release Train Cadence. What invariants, failure modes, and observability do you require?
interviewProblems.sampleDefense: Start from invariants, choose the pattern that preserves them, and add metrics for the known failure modes.
commonPitfalls: Optimizing throughput before defining correctness boundaries.

steps.title: 1. Normal Request Ingress
steps.explanation: A release train is a fixed-schedule software delivery model where releases depart on a predictable calendar cadence—shipping whatever features are complete and verified, while incomplete work waits for the next train.

steps.title: 2. Core Execution & State Lookup
steps.explanation: Canary Gate applies the primary invariant and coordinates with Production Fleet.

steps.title: 3. Scale Spike / Failure Injection
steps.explanation: Under a 10x burst, Production Fleet experiences contention and tail-latency amplification.

steps.title: 4. Mitigation & Steady Recovery
steps.explanation: Enforce automated branch cuts via CI (GitHub Actions/GitLab CI) and require VP/EM sign-off for any post-cut cherry-pick.

tipsAndTricks: Core mental model: Decouple deployment timing from feature completion: fix the release date, keep main deployable via feature flags, and never hold the train for one late pull request.
Avoid trap: Tying marketing launch dates directly to code-cut dates instead of decoupling code shipping from flag activation.
Avoid trap: Assigning a permanent manual 'release hero' instead of rotating a lightweight Release Captain role supported by automated CI scripts.
When to reach for it: Multiple squads ship into a shared monorepo, mobile binary (iOS/Android), or coupled platform where coordinated integration testing is required.

When to reach for it: External constraints—such as App Store/Play Store review windows (24–48 hours), enterprise customer change windows, or compliance sign-offs—prevent continuous per-commit deployment.

putItTogether.title: Putting Release Train Cadence Together
putItTogether.summary: Decouple deployment timing from feature completion: fix the release date, keep main deployable via feature flags, and never hold the train for one late pull request.
steps: Establish baseline invariants for Release Train Cadence before scaling.
Isolate hot paths with caching, backpressure, or partitioning.
Verify failure modes with synthetic load & chaos checks.
putItTogether.outcome: Cutting `release/2026.11` every other Monday at 10:00 UTC, running a 24-hour internal dogfood soak, and submitting Tuesday morning yields predictable Thursday 5%->100% phased rollouts and zero emergency scope-delay meetings.
